Does it track introductions? Weakly. On the days of the nine first detections behind the reference rate, the index of the county was 0.44 to 2.96, 1.45 on average, so those events came where the index was somewhat above average. In the check against 2026 the model's chances, which combine the index with the season and the county's size, ranked counties with no earlier case fairly well and counties with a first-wave case hardly at all.

In the app: the default for detections in nearby counties stays the value set by hand, 1.5. This page does not change it.

Not in the index: detections in Mexico, so a county on the border misses its southern neighbour. A first look at public sources (18 November 2026) found the Mexican animal-health agency's cumulative counts by state at nine irregular dates, the last on 15 July 2026, with none between 28 February and 15 July 2026. Over that gap the cumulative count for Tamaulipas, a Mexican state on the Texas border, went from 38 to 1,162. No public table by state and month was found, so Mexican cases are a known gap here, not an input. Also not in the index: premises locations; terrain, wind and animal movements. Checks made: a county's own cases do not enter its index, removing every case after a date leaves the index on that date unchanged, and the index averages 1 over the reference county-days. This year's weather

Using 2026 temperatures in place of the long-term normals changes the county result very little. The chance of freedom at the last round (day 360) stays at 0.853. The largest change at any round is 0.017 lower, at day 180 (November): 0.898 against 0.915.

Why so small: from June to September fly activity is already at its cap of 1 under the normals, and it stays there in 2026, so a hotter or cooler summer cannot move it. Only the autumn months can differ, and the chance of freedom forgets a past month within about two rounds. The months from December on are not yet observed and keep the normals.

Proposed: fly traps and wildlife findings as evidence

Proposed, not built. A design exists for letting fly traps and wildlife findings count as evidence. It is not accepted, neither build of the model implements it, and no number on this page uses it. The rule in force is unchanged. A positive wild fly capture counts as a detection; sterile flies are dyed and do not count. Empty traps give no credit (how infested farms are found).

What a reviewer would see: two more evidence streams beside owner reporting, each running all the time. One is fly traps. The other is wildlife and companion-animal findings: hunter harvest, roadkill, wildlife agency checks, and dogs seen at veterinary clinics. A finding by either stream would be a confirmed detection with the same consequences as an owner report. With both streams switched off, which is the default in the builds, every result is exactly as it is now.

Three inputs per stream, with the proposed starting value and the range to explore:

InputWhat it isFly trapsWildlife and companion animals
Coveragethe share of infested premises the stream could ever find0.5 (0.1 to 1)0.3 (0.05 to 0.8)
Ratefor a premises within reach, the chance per day of a confirmed finding0.005 per day, about 3.4 percent per week (0.001 to 0.07)0.01 per day (0.002 to 0.1)
Delaythe age of the infestation on the premises from which the stream can find it14 days (10 to 35)7 days (3 to 30)

What empty traps would earn: a little, and slowly. At the starting values a premises infested on day 0 would be found by traps with chance 0.04 by day 30, 0.16 by day 90 and 0.28 by day 180. For wildlife and companion-animal findings the same chances are 0.06, 0.17 and 0.25. An owner report comes within days. Nothing is earned before the delay has passed, because a premises sends out adult flies only after the larvae have left the wound and pupated.

What empty traps would not earn: more than the coverage. Coverage is a ceiling. A premises out of reach of the traps is never found by them, so however long the traps stay empty they cannot rule out more than the coverage share of infested premises. A worked example from the proposal: start with 3 expected undetected premises, switch off everything except traps, and give the traps a coverage of 0.5, a rate of 0.05 per day and a delay of 14 days. The chance the zone is free stays at 0.05 until day 14, climbs to 0.19 by day 60 and then levels off just under 0.223, however long the traps stay empty. With a coverage of 1 the same traps would take it toward 1. An empty trap says little unless the stated coverage supports it.

The starting values are guesses. Five of the six are marked guessed, and the trap delay is derived from development times. No source on file gives a measured chance that traps detect a wild population of this species at low density, and none gives a rate at which wildlife or dog cases reveal an infested premises. The trap rate on file rests on recapture of released sterile flies and on catches where the fly is established.

Not in the proposal: a trap that catches a fly arriving from outside when no premises is infested, wildlife as a reservoir with its own spread, trap placement, and a change of the rates with season.

The streams the model uses now are listed on the county scenario. What the model leaves out: what the model leaves out.

Introduction interval

Value: one new infested farm arrives in the zone about every 130 days. Evidence: counted from reports. Assumed: An active quarantine zone lies next to the zone for the whole period, and a rate counted per county applies to the zone unchanged.

The model assumes 130 days; the range explored is 50 to 400 days.

Prior in the ranking: log-uniform over 130 to 721 days, because the rate on record may be too high and by how much is not known (the first ranking drew 50 to 400 days). Sensitivity: rank 6 of 29 rows, county scenario (effect +0.058 on the chance of freedom at day 360).

Detail and sources

What this is: The average number of days between new infestations arriving in the zone from outside it (flies flying in, moved animals or wildlife), one rate for the whole zone. In the zone picture it is the "New arrivals from outside" input. It counts arrivals from outside the zone. As fitted, it also carries spread from infested areas next to the zone (see how the value was reached); the zone's own spread term is separate and has almost no effect on freedom.

Checked against the official record in this version: the first cases behind this count were taken from a public online encyclopedia's case table. The official record of confirmed detections, pulled on 17 November 2026, lists the same counties with the same totals through 31 August 2026. The nine counted introductions keep their dates, except the Starr County case, which moves by one day. The value is not recounted in this version, and the cases confirmed since 31 August are not in it (what changed, 17 November 2026).

Value: 130 d, range 50 to 400 d (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom +0.117.

What the value rests on: counted from reports The first cases were counted from news reports and a public case compilation, then divided by a time window and by a judged number of at-risk counties. The value fails the page's rule for a high-impact parameter.

Quote check on this card's sources: 4 quotes: 4 found word for word. See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

The chosen value of 130 days (range 50 to 400) applies to a free county next to an active zone. The AI literature review dated the first case in every Texas county in summer 2026 [C-2.1, C-2.2, C-2.7a, C-2.7b]. Six far-apart counties seeded within ten days of the first case, and one later far jump (Jim Hogg, 25 June), were set aside as spread that took place before anyone knew of the outbreak. Nine later first cases (20 June to 16 August) all bordered an active quarantine zone and were counted as introductions, so spread from infested areas next door is part of this rate. Nine events over the AI literature review's 85-day window, spread across 12 to 20 at-risk counties, give 0.005 to 0.009 introductions per county per day, which is a mean interval of 110 to 190 days, and 130 days was picked inside that span. The nine dates span 57 days (20 June to 16 August), and the review does not say what period the 85 days covers. Over 57 days the same arithmetic gives 76 to 127 days, which is below the chosen 130. If the rule is read literally, as a county sharing a border with a county that already had a case, Medina County would be dropped. None of its neighbours had a confirmed case by its first case on 24 June (Uvalde's first case came on 29 June), although Uvalde had been in a quarantine zone since 3 June [C-2.2]. That reading leaves eight events, or 0.0047 to 0.0078 per county per day over the 85 days, which is an interval of 128 to 213 days with the chosen 130 at the lower edge, according to the source census. The Medina date appears in the case compilation [C-2.1] and in a dated case list relaying the USDA dashboard [C-2.2], and the other news article cited with it gives no Medina date [C-2.7b]. The figure of 12 to 20 at-risk counties is the AI literature review's judgement, and no source gives the ring of at-risk counties. The evidence does not match the parameter exactly. A first case is dated by laboratory confirmation rather than by arrival, and a county is not necessarily the model's zone, where a larger zone means a shorter interval. The range ends are judgement. A model paper's seeding rate [C-2.6] was used only as a consistency check. This is the top parameter, accounting for about half the variance in six-month freedom, and it fails the page's own rule for high-impact parameters (step 4 of the review process), because its evidence is a public compilation and news reports, with no primary source and no expert elicitation. Official case records with dates would remedy that. Every case date behind the count comes from a public online encyclopedia's case table [C-2.1] and a syndicated news article [C-2.2], and no quote from these sources carries those dates. The 4 quotes found on this card's sources give context (long-distance spread [C-2.4] and a model's seeding rate [C-2.6]) rather than the dates that were counted.

What the sources do not tell us

No official linkage of any 2026 case is in the sources reviewed, so the sources do not say which introductions were moved animals and which were flies, or whether the at-risk ring really held 12 to 20 counties.

Owner reporting delay

Value: 3 days on average from the owner noticing a wound to a confirmed detection. Evidence: little data. Assumed: The value and the upper end of the range are judgement above a floor set by three timed cases.

There is little good data for this value. The model assumes 3 days; the range explored is 1 to 12.5 days.

Prior in the ranking: lognormal with 5th and 95th percentiles 1 and 12.5 days, because a delay is positive and the reports give a short and a long case. Sensitivity: rank 4 of 29 rows, county scenario (effect −0.075 on the chance of freedom at day 360).

Detail and sources

What this is: How fast a wound the owner has noticed becomes a confirmed detection, set as a daily rate; one over the rate is the mean delay in days. In the model pictures it is part of "Owner reports a wound" on the farm picture and the "Owner reports" input on the zone picture. It starts when the owner notices (the time for a wound to become visible and to be noticed is not in it) and it ends at confirmation, not at the owner's call: the model treats a detection as a confirmed one and has no separate laboratory step, so the time from the call to laboratory confirmation sits inside this delay.

What the delay covers

The domain experts break the time from a fly laying eggs to a confirmed case into four parts. The model lumps the last three into this one delay, so it covers more than the owner's wait:

  1. Fly to noticing: from egg laying until the owner sees a wound. Not in this delay: the latent time and the chance a sick animal is noticed cover it.
  2. Owner waits: the owner has seen something but looks closely days later. In this delay.
  3. Veterinary sampling: a veterinarian or official comes out to sample and ships it. In this delay.
  4. Laboratory: from receipt to confirmation, "several days" (domain experts; no written source). One 2026 preprint reports 3 to 7 day testing bottlenecks (Garcia, abstract only, a background claim, not a measurement). In this delay.

The parts are not built up into the 3 days.

Outside the range: the naive-area figure on this card (Florida 2016, a mean of about 14 days) lies above the range's 12.5-day end, and the APHIS response strategy (A-1.1, page 18 of the PDF) records that in the 2016 to 2017 Florida outbreak samples were not sent to NVSL for identification until 84 days after presumptive positive identification by local veterinarians. The range does not cover it.

Value: 0.33 /d (mean 3 d), range 0.08 to 1.0 /d (mean delay 1 to 12.5 d) (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom -0.089.

What the value rests on: judgement within data Three timed cases set a floor of about 1.5 to 2 days. The 3 days and the 12.5-day upper end are judgement.

Quote check on this card's sources: 7 quotes: 6 found word for word, 1 near match. See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

The chosen value is a mean delay of 3 days (a rate of 0.33 per day), with a range of 1 to 12.5 days (rates of 1.0 to 0.08 per day). Three timed cases were found. In the first, the manager of a ranch in Zavala County found a calf's wound on a routine check, and the laboratory confirmed it 2.5 days later [B-3.7]. This is the only case timed from the owner. In the second, a household dog from Lea County, New Mexico, was seen at a veterinary clinic in Andrews County, Texas, on Saturday 6 June 2026 [B-3.19]. The news report gives confirmation on Monday 8 June, but a case table based on APHIS data dates it 7 June [C-2.1], so the interval is 1 to 2 days. Its clock starts at the clinic, so the owner's own delay is missing, and because the dog's travel history is unknown, the case is perhaps better read as evidence of an introduction. In the third, at Sabinas Hidalgo, Mexico, a heifer recently moved to a certified feedlot was detected officially on 20 September 2025 and confirmed on 21 September, an interval of 1 day [B-3.10, B-3.9]. It was not an owner report, so it times only the sampling and laboratory steps. Texas rules ask for a report within 24 hours of a suspect case [B-3.8], but this states what owners are required to do and is not a measured delay. The evidence does not match the parameter exactly. Two of the three intervals leave out the owner's step and therefore understate the delay, so their average of about 1.5 to 2 days is a floor rather than an estimate. All three cases come from areas on alert during an active response, whereas the six-month scenario applies the same 3 days after release, when alertness may have fallen. The AI literature review's alternative for a naive area, from Florida 2016, is a rate of 0.07 per day (a mean of about 14 days), and it is not used in the headline estimate. The 3 days and the 12.5-day upper end are the AI literature review's judgement.

What the sources do not tell us

No per-case dates of noticing, reporting and confirmation are in the sources reviewed, so the sources do not say how long owners actually wait between first noticing a wound and calling it in.

Zone clearance time

Value: 21 days on average from a new detection to the release of each farm still counted, and not used before a detection. Evidence: bounded by published sources. Assumed: The agency release rule for found and treated farms sets the clock for every counted farm.

The model assumes 21 days; the range explored is 7 to 40 days.

Prior in the ranking: none drawn. Sensitivity: not in the ranking. Zone clearance is switched off in the county scenario, so this input is a fixed setting.

Detail and sources

What this is: The average number of days before a counted farm is removed from the zone's infested count by clearance. It plays no part in any freedom number: clearance is off for farms nobody has found, which leave the count only when their own infestation has run its course (see the equations card). The 21 days is used only after a new confirmed detection, as the release clock: from then on each counted farm leaves at that rate, standing for the release rule for found and treated farms. The model pictures do not draw the release clock; the clock starts at a confirmed detection, a farm drawn as "Found" on the zone picture.

Value: 21 d, after a new detection only (off before), range 7 to 40 d (90 percent interval); no effect on six-month freedom (not drawn in the ranking).

What the value rests on: judgement within data The value rests on an agency release rule and on news snapshots of active cases, which time paperwork rather than biology, and the tails are judgement. It is used only after a new detection, so it does not move freedom.

Quote check on this card's sources: 8 quotes: 7 found word for word, 1 near match. See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 21 days, with a range of 7 to 40. It sets only the release clock after a new detection, so it does not move freedom. It rests on two kinds of evidence. The first is the release rule. A treated animal is re-inspected 24 hours after treatment and released once no live larvae remain and an official veterinarian signs off [C-3.1], and the Green Book keeps animals in quarantine until the wounds heal [C-3.2]. The second is how long Texas 2026 cases stayed on the active list, read from news snapshots of active counts on 30 June, 6 August, 18 August and 3 September [C-2.2, B-2.22, B-2.17, A-3.18]. Each case is only bracketed between two dates (for example 25 to 62 days, or 0 to 19 days) and is not timed. A fit that treats each of 46 Texas cases as such a bracket (interval-censored maximum likelihood) gives a mean of 18.7 days with an exponential curve and 20.1 days with a lognormal curve (median 14.8 days), and the spread is wide. The count of four active cases on 3 September is the AI literature review's reading, because that tracker page has since been overwritten. The evidence does not match the parameter exactly, because it times the administrative clock rather than the biology. The first Texas calf's wound healed in a week [B-3.7], and its case was off the active list by 30 June [C-2.2], at most 27 days after its confirmation on 3 June, but no source says how much sooner it left the list. The times are also per animal case and interval-censored, not per premises. A 21-day Texas release rule seen only in a search summary could not be verified. The tails (7 and 40 days) are judgement, and the AI literature review rated them as low confidence.

What the sources do not tell us

The release rule and the case lists time paperwork rather than fly output, so the sources do not say when a cleared premises actually stops producing flies, which is what matters for spread.

Within-premises recovery time

Value: 7 days on average for an infested animal to stop carrying larvae. Evidence: bounded by published sources. Assumed: The value is a mix of treated and untreated animals, and the share treated early is not known.

The model assumes 7 days; the range explored is 3 to 15 days.

Prior in the ranking: lognormal with 5th and 95th percentiles 3 and 15 days, because a time is positive and the sources give a low and a high. Sensitivity: rank 8 of 29 rows, county scenario (effect +0.034 on the chance of freedom at day 360).

Detail and sources

What this is: The average number of days one animal carries live larvae, until treatment, the larvae leaving, or death ends it. In the farm picture it is the Infested to Recovered step. It moves animals, and it also sets when a farm nobody has found leaves the zone's infested count: at the end of its infestation's course, 166 days after infestation at the central values, or about 9 days at a 3-day recovery, when the infestation dies out on its own. That course is an assumption about one farm's current infestation, with little data behind it. New infestations can still arrive.

Value: 7 d, range 3 to 15 d (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom +0.015.

What the value rests on: judgement within data The sources bound the treated and untreated courses, and the 7-day mix of the two is a modelling choice.

Quote check on this card's sources: 12 quotes: 10 found word for word, 2 near matches. See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 7 days, with a range of 3 to 15. Larvae feed for 5 to 7 days after hatching and then leave the wound [A-3.1, A-3.2, A-3.4]. Untreated wounds attract more egg-laying, and the animal dies in 5 to 10 days [A-3.4], 7 to 10 days [A-3.7], 7 to 14 days [A-3.8], or one to two weeks [A-3.1]. The AI literature review put the untreated larvae-bearing period at 6 to 12 days, with a central value of 10. In a trial, doramectin given 2 hours before first-stage larvae were placed in wounds cleared them within 24 to 48 hours [A-3.13]. That trial tested preventive dosing against young larvae rather than treatment of an established wound, so it bounds the treated course only loosely, and the federal procedure's re-inspection 24 hours after treatment [C-3.1] is closer. On that reading, an animal found on day 3 to 5 and treated carries larvae for 3 to 6 days. The 7 days is a mix of treated and untreated animals under surveillance, and the mix is a modelling choice rather than data. Figures that time something else were set aside as too long. These are the 15 to 17 days of a Mexican model's "infection process" [A-3.12] and the roughly 22 days of Mexico's active-case list [A-3.17], both of which run to wound healing. The model paper gives no end point for its infection process, and reading it as running to wound healing is the AI literature review's interpretation. A different value applies in one case. If the model already removes reported animals by treatment, the AI literature review recommends 10 days (6 to 17) for the undetected course instead.

What the sources do not tell us

The files do not give the real share of infested animals that are treated early rather than left alone, which sets the 7-day mix.

Chance the owner notices a wound

Value: 0.70, the chance for each animal with a visible wound that the owner notices it. Evidence: no data: assumed. Assumed: An alert owner notices most visible wounds.

There is no data for this value. The model assumes 0.70; the range explored is 0.45 to 0.90.

Prior in the ranking: beta with 5th and 95th percentiles 0.45 and 0.9, because the value is a share and no source narrows it further. Sensitivity: rank 12 of 29 rows, county scenario (effect +0.018 on the chance of freedom at day 360).

Detail and sources

What this is: The chance that an owner notices a visible screwworm wound on an infested animal. In the model pictures it is part of "Owner reports a wound" on the farm picture and the "Owner reports" input on the zone picture. It applies only to wounds that have already become visible (the visible-wound ramp comes before it); the time from noticing to confirmation is the separate reporting delay. In the model this chance applies to each animal on the farm that has a visible wound. The more animals have visible wounds, the more likely it is that the owner has noticed at least one of them, and the farm reports at the reporting rate multiplied by that likelihood (the equation is shown below). The chance is therefore not a single decision, made once, about whether a wound will ever be noticed. While its wounds stay visible, the farm can still be reported on any later day.

Where it enters the model: The owner-report rate of a farm infested τ days ago is h(τ) = ρr × [1 − (1 − ρa pclin(τ))N], where ρa is this chance, ρr is the reporting rate, pclin(τ) is the share of animals with a visible wound, and N is the number of animals on the farm. It is the last equation in the detection part of the model's equations.

Value: 0.70, range 0.45 to 0.90 (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom +0.028.

What the value rests on: guessed No study measures this chance, and no source on this card informs it directly. The value is a judgement made with indirect numbers in view.

Quote check on this card's sources: 7 quotes: 6 found word for word, 1 not found (not shown). See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

No source on this card measures or directly informs this chance, so the chosen value of 0.70 and its range of 0.45 to 0.90 are a judgement. The sources describe related quantities, which are set out below together with the reason each one does not give the chance the model needs. Mexico handled 10,511 animal myiasis reports from 1 January 2024 to 1 November 2025, and larvae from 9,049 of them were identified as screwworm [B-2.7]. Set against the 9,574 cases that the same bulletin confirms to the same end date (counted from 21 November 2024, when the outbreak's case count starts), the ratio is about 95 percent. This ratio compares identifications from reports with confirmed cases. It is not the share of cases found through reports, because one case can give several reports and the two counts start on different dates. It shows that most cases are found through owners and veterinarians, but it cannot say how many infested animals nobody reported, because those animals appear in neither count. In Florida in 2016, 3 of 9 pet cases (33 percent) surfaced only through a later questionnaire [B-2.1]. These were animals that veterinarians had seen, so the figure measures missed reporting in a naive area rather than owners failing to notice a wound. For wild Key deer, biologists estimated one undetected death for each known one [B-2.2], which describes the finding of carcasses in wildlife rather than a handled herd. Handling frequency comes from a 2015 online forum thread of small cattle producers, with answers ranging from daily to weekly [B-2.18], and from a recommendation to check animals daily [B-2.19]. The AI literature review's tally of 17 US posters in that thread does not reproduce, because the saved page has about 15 answers that give a frequency, two of them from Canada. None of these numbers is the per-animal chance the model needs. The central value and both range ends are judgement, and the recorded verdict is guessed.

What the sources do not tell us

No study in the sources reviewed measures what fraction of infested animals in an alert commercial herd go unnoticed.

Within-premises doubling time

Value: 3.6 days for the number of infested animals on a farm to double, before any recover. Evidence: converted from a related setting. Assumed: Growth rates of wild deer deaths and of fly populations apply to spread between animals on one farm.

The model assumes 3.6 days; the range explored is 3.2 to 3.9 days.

Prior in the ranking: not drawn directly. It is derived in each draw from the observed doubling time (lognormal, 5th and 95th percentiles 9 and 20 days) and the recovery time, so each draw matches the observed doubling (resulting range 1.8 to 6 days). Sensitivity: rank 7 of 29 rows, county scenario (effect +0.035 on the chance of freedom at day 360).

Detail and sources

What this is: How fast infestation spreads between animals on one farm, set as a doubling time before any animals recover. In the farm picture it is the Susceptible to Latent step, driven by the "their flies lay eggs on more animals" loop from Infested. It stands in for the local flies; the model has no fly population and no pupal stage.

What it implies (derived, not an input): this value is a gross rate, before animals recover. With latent time 2 days and recovery 7 days at their central values, the net doubling time of a farm's infestation is about 19 days, and each infested animal leads to 1.35 more (the outbreak on a farm grows only above 1). Across this card's range (3.2 to 3.9 days) that number runs from 1.24 to 1.52, above 1 across the whole range (net doubling about 13 to 27 days). The derivation above leaves out the 2-day latent stage, which slows early growth, so this net figure is longer than the net doubling the value was derived from.

Value: 3.6 d, range 3.2 to 3.9 d (at the central recovery time) (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom +0.014.

What the value rests on: converted from a related setting The value is converted by a formula from the growth rates of wild deer deaths and of fly populations, and it is applied to spread between animals on one farm. There is no direct measurement.

Quote check on this card's sources: 10 quotes: 10 found word for word. See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 3.6 days, with a range of 3.2 to 3.9. It is derived rather than observed. Observed doublings of case counts are net of recovery. The uncontrolled Key deer deaths (4, 7, 20 and 96 per month, July to October 2016) double every 13 to 20 days [A-5.8]. A five-fold rise per fly generation, which was Knipling's design assumption [A-5.2], over a generation of about 21 days [A-5.4] doubles every 9 days. A fly-population model gives a potential doubling time of 14 days [A-5.1]. The model's parameter is the gross rate, so the recovery rate was added back with the formula gross doubling = 1 / (1/net doubling + 1/(0.69 x recovery time)). With a recovery time of 7 to 14 days, this gives 3.2 to 7.7 days across the AI literature review's table, with a central value of 4.5. The model's own within-premises recovery time is 7 days, not about 14, so the value is derived at 7 days. Net doublings of 9, 13.4 and 20 days give 3.15, 3.56 and 3.90 days, hence the central value of 3.6 and the range of 3.2 to 3.9. The value is tied to the recovery time. Across recovery times of 3 to 15 days the consistent value runs from 1.7 to 6.8 days, and in the ranking it is derived in each draw from a sampled net doubling (9 to 20 days) and that draw's recovery time. The evidence does not match the parameter exactly. The deer series counts deaths of wild deer across whole islands, and the other two sources describe fly-population growth, not animals on one premises. The same report and series is also the main input to the zone doubling time [C-1.4], which describes spread between farms. The formula is the AI literature review's, and because the model's instant recruitment ignores the 18 to 24 day fly generation, early growth runs fast. The Texas 2026 outbreak (47 cases on 38 premises) [A-5.13a] was used as a consistency check only.

What the sources do not tell us

No direct measurement of spread between animals on one premises is in the sources reviewed.

Share of wounds visible

Value: 0.9, the share of infested animals whose wound ever becomes visible. Evidence: little data. Assumed: Few infestations stay hidden, as estimated from tallies of cases that were found.

There is little good data for this value. The model assumes 0.9; the range explored is 0.75 to 0.98.

Prior in the ranking: beta with 5th and 95th percentiles 0.75 and 0.98, because the value is a share, and a few indirect figures and judgement put it high. Sensitivity: rank 11 of 29 rows, county scenario (effect +0.019 on the chance of freedom at day 360).

Detail and sources

What this is: The share of infested animals whose wound eventually becomes visible to someone looking carefully; the rest sit in hidden places such as nostrils, genitals or deep pockets. The model pictures do not draw visible wounds; this share acts through "Owner reports a wound" on the farm picture, on animals at the Infested step. It acts on owner reporting only; inspection uses its own chance, the inspection sensitivity.

Value: 0.9, range 0.75 to 0.98 (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom +0.014.

What the value rests on: judgement within data No study counts hidden infestations, and the value is an estimate from site tallies of cases that were found.

Quote check on this card's sources: 6 quotes: 5 found word for word, 1 not found (not shown). See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 0.9, with a range of 0.75 to 0.98. No study counts how many infestations stay hidden on a careful look. Reference texts all name the same hard sites, namely the nostrils, anus, prepuce, vagina and deep pocket wounds, where slight movement may be the only sign [A-4.1, A-4.2, A-4.3]. A Colombian cattle study lists barbed-wire injuries in 32.7 percent of 49 cases and the navel and scrotum in 18.4 percent each [A-4.4], and the AI literature review read this as 70 percent or more of cases at plainly visible sites. Newborns are an estimated 80 percent of potential livestock cases, mostly at the navel [A-4.7]. The evidence does not match the parameter exactly. A site tally includes only cases that someone found, so hidden cases are missing from it and the visible share is pushed up. The Colombian quote was also not found verbatim, and because wire injury is a cause while the navel and scrotum are sites, the sum may double count. The 0.9 and its range are an educated estimate, as the AI literature review itself calls them. The hidden share here (10 percent at the central value) and the 15 to 25 percent at hidden sites assumed on the inspection sensitivity card are two separate judgements, and they do not agree.

What the sources do not tell us

No study in the sources reviewed counts how many infestations stay hidden on a careful look at a US herd.

Mean latent time

Value: 2 days on average from eggs laid in a wound to larvae present. Evidence: bounded by published sources. Assumed: The same latent time holds at Texas temperatures.

The model assumes 2 days; the range explored is 1 to 3 days.

Prior in the ranking: gamma with 5th and 95th percentiles 1 and 3 days, because a time is positive and the sources give a low and a high. Sensitivity: rank 14 of 29 rows, county scenario (effect −0.016 on the chance of freedom at day 360).

What this is: The average number of days from eggs laid in a wound to larvae present and visible. In the farm picture it is the Latent to Infested step. An animal still in the eggs-laid state cannot be found by inspection and does not pass infestation on.

Detail and sources

Value: 2 d, range 1 to 3 d (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom -0.019.

What the value rests on: judgement within data Life-history summaries agree on 1 to 3 days. The two trials time the interval from wounding to detection, so they bound the value only loosely.

Quote check on this card's sources: 7 quotes: 6 found word for word, 1 not found (not shown). See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 2 days, with a range of 1 to 3. Eggs hatch in 10 to 12 hours [A-1.1], 12 to 24 hours [A-1.2, A-1.3] or 10 to 21 hours [A-1.4]. Larvae are hard to see for the first day or two [A-1.3] and are visible by the third day [A-1.1], and disease can show as early as 1 to 2 days after egg laying [A-1.2]. Two field trials with regular inspection found infestations by day 3 to 5 after wounding in Mexico [A-1.7] and in 9 of 10 untreated castration wounds by the day-3 check in Argentina [A-1.8]. The early detections in Mexico were in the ivermectin group, where the drug failed, and the untreated controls were infested by day 8, as on the clinical onset card. There is a minor mismatch between the evidence and the parameter. The trials count from the day of wounding rather than the day the eggs were laid, so day 3 to 5 is an upper bound on latency plus the time to notice. The Mexican authors also found larvae older than expected, which suggests that young larvae were being missed. The life-history sources agree on 1 to 3 days, and the trials are consistent with that span without timing it, so the value of 2 days (1 to 3) is supported. The range ends match the span of the life-history sources. The Argentine quote was not found verbatim in the source.

What the sources do not tell us

Temperature is noted to move hatching by hours, but no Texas measurement is in the sources reviewed, so the sources do not say how latency shifts with Texas temperatures.

Mean clinical onset time

Value: 3 days for an infested wound to become obvious to an observer. Evidence: little data. Assumed: The clock runs from the day the farm was infested, which is earlier than the reviewed value intended.

There is little good data for this value. The model assumes 3 days; the range explored is 1.5 to 6 days.

Prior in the ranking: gamma with 5th and 95th percentiles 1.5 and 6 days, because a time is positive and the few figures give a low and a high. Sensitivity: rank 15 of 29 rows, county scenario (effect −0.015 on the chance of freedom at day 360).

Detail and sources

What this is: How many days it takes for an infested wound to become obvious to an observer; the visible share of wounds ramps up on this time scale. The model pictures do not draw visible wounds; this time acts through "Owner reports a wound" on the farm picture. Its clock runs from the day the farm was infested, not from the day each animal first carried larvae, and it feeds owner reporting only.

Value: 3 d, range 1.5 to 6 d (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom +0.000.

What the value rests on: judgement within data No study measures it, and the trials only bound it. There is also a known mismatch, because the model's clock starts earlier than the review intended.

Quote check on this card's sources: 5 quotes: 4 found word for word, 1 not found (not shown). See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 3 days, with a range of 1.5 to 6. No study measures how long owners take to notice a wound. Under daily chute inspection, infestations were found on day 3 to 5 after wounding [A-2.4], and 9 of 10 untreated castration wounds were obviously infested at the day-3 check [A-2.5]. Both trials looked on fixed days (the Argentine trial on days 3, 6 and 13 only), and the Mexican detections on day 3 to 5 were in the ivermectin group, where the drug failed. The abstract gives untreated controls infested on day 8. The trials therefore show wounds obvious by day 3 to 5 after wounding and say nothing about shorter times. On extensive range, herds are mustered only every few days [A-2.7], and observers rely on odour [A-2.2] and on animals leaving the herd [A-2.3]. A mean of 3 days after larvae appear, with a range of 1.5 to 6 days, was chosen to span both settings, and the range ends are judgement. There is a mismatch between the review and the model. The AI literature review meant 3 days from the start of the larvae-bearing stage, but the model's ramp runs on the premises' age since infestation, which already includes the latent period of roughly 2 days. In the model, wounds therefore become obvious sooner after larvae appear than the review intended, by about the 2-day latent time, which makes owner detection look faster and freedom higher.

What the sources do not tell us

No study in the sources reviewed measures how many days a Texas rancher on extensive range actually takes to spot a wound.

Lockdown spread multiplier

Value: 0.25, the factor applied to spread between farms after the first detection. Evidence: little data. Assumed: More sterile flies and tighter movement controls cut spread by this factor, and the cut is never lifted.

There is little good data for this value. The model assumes 0.25; the range explored is 0.07 to 0.6.

Prior in the ranking: lognormal with 5th and 95th percentiles 0.07 and 0.6, because the value is positive and only its rough size is known. Sensitivity: rank 27 of 29 rows, county scenario (effect −0.001 on the chance of freedom at day 360, inside the noise band).

Detail and sources

What this is: The factor by which spread between farms is cut once the first detection is confirmed, standing for sterile-fly releases plus movement controls; 1 means no cut. In the zone picture it is the dot-dash "Spread reduced after lockdown" arrow, which the "Initiate lockdown" box switches on once a farm is found. In the model's formula it cuts spread between farms only; introductions from outside and spread inside a farm are not changed. Every freedom number on this page is computed given no confirmed detection, so this cut never acts on them.

Value: 0.25, range 0.07 to 0.6 (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom +0.006.

What the value rests on: operating setting It is a control setting informed by the sterile-fly literature, and it has almost no effect in this model.

Quote check on this card's sources: 9 quotes: 7 found word for word, 2 with no full text to check. See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 0.25, with a range of 0.07 to 0.6. It is set as an operating setting rather than taken from the literature, and it has not yet been formally extracted from the literature. Sterile flies released at a ratio of 9 sterile flies to 1 wild fly leave only 10 percent of females laying fertile eggs, and a ratio of at least 10 to 1 is the working rule [C-4.1]. The effect lags by a fly generation, and in Florida the last fertile fly was caught 27 days after releases began [C-4.4]. Averaging over a 90-day lockdown of about four life cycles, the AI literature review computed about 0.3 for the fly part, using per-generation factors (1, 0.15, 0.03, 0.01) whose origin is not in the sources reviewed. Movement permits cut the animal-movement part to perhaps 0.1 to 0.3, which is a judgement. The Green Book says that long-distance movement of the fly is generally a result of moving an infested animal [C-2.4] (C-2.4 and C-4.7a are entries for the same document). That statement covers long-distance spread only, not local spread by flies, which permits do not touch. Texas 2026 active-case counts [C-2.2, B-2.22, B-2.17, A-3.18] gave 0.06 to 0.5. The evidence does not match the parameter exactly, because Texas already had sterile flies from February, so its starting point was not uncontrolled. In this model structure, spread between premises is almost nil, so this setting has almost no effect.

What the sources do not tell us

No series in the sources reviewed shows the effect of a response that starts from no sterile flies at all, which is the clean before-and-after comparison that the setting assumes.

Zone doubling time

Value: 24 days for the number of infested farms to double with no control. Evidence: converted from a related setting. Assumed: The growth of one series of wild deer deaths applies to spread between farms.

The model assumes 24 days; the range explored is 6 to 25 days.

Prior in the ranking: lognormal with 5th and 95th percentiles 6 and 25 days, because a time is positive and the converted figures give a low and a high. Sensitivity: rank 28 of 29 rows, county scenario (effect −0.001 on the chance of freedom at day 360, inside the noise band).

Detail and sources

What this is: How fast the number of infested farms in the zone would grow with no control, set as a doubling time. In the zone picture it is the "Spread between farms" input, drawn as the solid orange arrow in the farm grid (legend: "Between-farm spread"); its rate is multiplied by the share of animals carrying larvae on the infested farms. It has almost no effect on the estimate.

Value: 24 d, range 6 to 25 d (not re-centred) (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom -0.005.

What the value rests on: converted from a related setting The value is converted by a formula from the growth of one series of wild deer deaths and applied to spread between farms, and it has almost no effect in this model.

Quote check on this card's sources: 6 quotes: 3 found word for word, 2 near matches, 1 not found (not shown). See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 24 days, with a range of 6 to 25. It is derived from one series. Key deer deaths rose from 4 in July to 20 in September 2016 with no control, a net growth of 0.026 per day, which is a doubling every 26 days, and the period from July to October gives 20 days [C-1.4]. The AI literature review took a net value of 24 days. With zone clearance off before a detection, the net figure of about 24 days is the consistent value. The 54 to 139 days in a fly-population model [C-1.1] was set aside, because it comes from mark-recapture work on an established Costa Rican population in balance [C-1.2] rather than from an invasion. Mexico's national counts, which doubled every 63 and then every 144 days, bound the value from above [C-1.5]. The evidence does not match the parameter exactly, because the series counts wild deer deaths on islands rather than infested premises. The same Key deer series, from the same report, is also the main input to the within-premises doubling time [A-5.8], which describes a different process. The range ends are judgement. In this model, this value has almost no effect on the estimate.

What the sources do not tell us

The only series in the sources reviewed is of wild deer, so the sources do not say how fast infested premises multiply in an uncontrolled US livestock setting.

Inspection sensitivity

Value: 0.85, the chance an inspector finds an infested animal that is examined. Evidence: no data: assumed. Assumed: A trained inspector misses few infested animals among those examined.

There is no data for this value. The model assumes 0.85; the range explored is 0.65 to 0.95.

Prior in the ranking: beta with 5th and 95th percentiles 0.65 and 0.95, because the value is a share and judgement puts it high. Sensitivity: rank 23 of 29 rows, county scenario (effect +0.007 on the chance of freedom at day 360, inside the noise band).

Detail and sources

What this is: The chance that an inspection finds an active infestation on one infested animal it examines. In the farm picture it acts through "Inspection: a sample of animals", and in the zone picture through the "Inspection rounds" input: it feeds the chance an inspected infested farm is found; one the round does not find is drawn as "Missed". It applies only to animals carrying larvae (eggs not yet hatched are missed) and plays no part in owner reporting.

Value: 0.85, range 0.65 to 0.95 (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom +0.002.

What the value rests on: guessed No study measures it for this fly, and the value is a weighted guess.

Quote check on this card's sources: 6 quotes: 6 found word for word. See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 0.85, with a range of 0.65 to 0.95. No study measures it for this fly, and the value is a weighted guess. Inspection protocols require a whole-body look that includes the mucous membranes and genitals [B-1.2], larvae are visible from day 3, and deep wounds may show only movement [B-1.1]. The AI literature review assumed that 15 to 25 percent of infestations sit at hidden sites, based on Mexican cases found in an ear and a prepuce [B-1.7] and on the protocol lists. With a sensitivity of about 0.6 at hidden sites and 0.95 at visible sites, this gives 0.85 to 0.9. The 15 to 25 percent, the 0.6 and the 0.95 are judgement, not measurements. The hidden share of 15 to 25 percent does not agree with the 10 percent hidden share on the share of wounds visible card, and the two are separate judgements. The nearest data are for the Old World screwworm, for which herd inspections detected it 30 percent of the time at low fly density and every time at high density [B-1.4]. The evidence does not match the parameter exactly, because those figures are herd-level detection per round for a different fly, driven by how many animals were infested, rather than the per-animal chance the model uses.

What the sources do not tell us

No study in the sources reviewed measures how often a trained US inspector misses an infested animal in a chute.

Detail and sources

What this is: How many days pass between the owner's close looks at the animals. A wound that has become visible waits for the owner's next close look, on average half this interval, and then for the owner reporting delay. A value of 0 means a close look every day, which reproduces the model before this version. In the pictures: "The owner's next close look" on the detection picture.

Where it enters the model: The effective owner reporting rate is ρr,eff = 1 / (1 / ρr + Tlook / 2), where Tlook is this interval and ρr is the owner reporting rate. It takes the place of ρr in the owner-report rate h(τ). It is written in the detection part of the model's equations. At the scenario values the mean delay from a visible wound to a report is 3 + 3.5 = 6.5 days.

Its effect: on the six-month scenario the model estimate of the chance the zone is free at day 180 (draft) is 89 percent at 7 days and 93 percent at 0 days, computed with the analytic (closed-form) build of this version.

Share of the sterile-fly release target being met

Value: 0.3 of the sterile-fly release target is met. Evidence: little data. Assumed: Production against the planned level stands in for release over the county, and the same share held when the introduction rate was counted.

There is little good data for this value. The model assumes 0.3; the range explored is 0 to 1.5.

Detail and sources

What this is: How much of the sterile-fly release target is being met, as a share, the same for every county. The reference is 0.3, the share assumed for the period in which the introduction rate was counted. At 0.3 the sterile-fly factor is 1. Above 0.3 fewer flies arriving are fertile, and below it more are. In the pictures: the "Sterile-fly release share" dial on "Flies arriving" on the introductions picture.

Where it enters the model: With x this share and κ the strength of the sterile-fly effect, the fertile share of matings is 1 / (1 + κ x), and the sterile-fly factor is S = (1 + 0.3 κ) / (1 + κ x). The formula is on the introductions card and in the model's equations.

Value: 0.3, range 0 to 1.5 (range to explore); its effect on the county scenario is in the ranking for this version.

What the value rests on: judgement within data Public production figures against a planned level of about 500 million a week, used here as the target, give about 0.3. Release records are not public.

See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

The value rests on public production figures set against a planned production level, used here as the target. The plant in Panama produces about 100 million sterile flies a week (APHIS sterile-fly production and dispersal page, modified 21 October 2026). A news report of 10 November 2026, citing a television station, puts the plant in southern Mexico at about 40 million a week; this figure is weaker. The programme says production will approach about 500 million a week once its investments are complete (APHIS screwworm page, modified 10 November 2026). That gives 140 of 500, or 28 percent, rounded to 0.3. All three pages were read on 18 November 2026. Production is not release over a given county: actual release numbers by area are not public, so the range stays wide. The same value is used as the reference. This assumes the shortfall was the same while the 2026 cases were counted, which is not known. The response to coverage follows the ratio rule of Knipling, as reported by Krafsur (1994).

What the sources do not tell us

No public record gives the number of sterile flies released against the target, by area and month. The figure for the plant in Mexico comes from a news report.

What this is: A multiplier on the flies arriving and the moved animals. A value of 1 stands for the detections in nearby counties in summer 2026, when the reference rate was counted. The county scenario uses 1.5, and the earlier six-month scenario does not use this input. The user sets it by hand. Counties to the south should weigh most, because seasonal spread runs northward. In the pictures: the two "Nearby detections" dials, on "Flies arriving" and on "Moved animals", on the introductions picture.

Value: 1.5, range 0 to 5 (range to explore); its effect on the county scenario is in the ranking for this version.

What the value rests on: judgement within data The default follows a ratio of case counts in the official record, and the distance that counts as nearby is judgement. The rate is assumed proportional to the multiplier, which is set by hand.

See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

No formula in the literature turns detections nearby into an introduction rate, so the rate is assumed proportional to this multiplier. The official record shows that pressure has not been constant: 4 confirmed cases in August 2026, 34 in October and 57 in the first 16 days of November. The default of the county scenario was raised from 1 to 1.5 to follow that record. The official record of confirmed detections, pulled on 17 November 2026, lists 23 confirmed animal cases within 400 km of the county in the 30 days to 16 November 2026. In the summer, from 1 June to 31 August 2026, it lists 47 there, which is 15.3 per 30 days. The ratio is 1.5. Within 300 km the ratio is 1.2. Over every county in the record it is 5.6, and most of those cases are far to the west, in New Mexico, Arizona and far west Texas. The choice of 400 km is judgement. The data are thin: one 30-day count, and the ratio depends strongly on the distance chosen. The value is still a multiplier set by hand. It does not weigh counties to the south more. An index computed from the detections by distance and direction now exists beside it and is not the default.

What the sources do not tell us

No source relates the number, distance and direction of nearby detections to the rate of introductions.

How well preventive treatment protects an animal

Value: 0.3, how much a preventive treatment lowers the chance that a treated animal becomes infested. Evidence: little data. Assumed: Protection is partial, as a judgement between trials that disagree.

There is little good data for this value. The model assumes 0.3; the range explored is 0 to 1.

Prior in the ranking: uniform over 0 to 0.9, because there is no information to prefer any value in the range. Sensitivity: rank 16 of 29 rows, county scenario (effect +0.015 on the chance of freedom at day 360).

Detail and sources

What this is: How much a preventive treatment lowers the chance that a treated animal becomes infested, from 0 (no protection) to 1 (full protection), averaged over the time between treatments. It matters only when some animals are treated. In the pictures: not drawn; it sets how strongly the "Preventive treatment" dial acts on the introductions picture.

Value: 0.3, range 0 to 1 (range to explore); its effect on the county scenario is in the ranking for this version.

What the value rests on: judgement within data Trials disagree, and only their abstracts were read. The value is a judgement between them.

See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

The trials disagree. Trials of doramectin injection in the 1990s, with induced infestation, found protection for about 14 to 21 days (Moya-Borja and others 1993 and 1997; Anziani and others 2000). Two trials under natural exposure found little or no protection in the first 3 to 14 days (Muchiut and others 2025; de Freitas and others 2026). Only the abstracts of these trials were read. The value of 0.3 is a judgement between the two groups of trials.

What the sources do not tell us

No statement of protection days on a product label for the United States was found, and no trial in the sources reviewed is from Texas.

A 2025 to 2026 cattle trial in Chiapas, Mexico, with deliberate wounds checked daily. The earliest infestations, days 3 to 5, were in the ivermectin group, where the drug failed; the abstract gives two untreated controls infested on day 8 in the first period and one control case in the second.

Deliberate wounds in a treatment trial, but infestation came from wild flies (natural exposure).

Open the source

What it reports: Day 3 (2 animals), day 4 (4), day 5 (3) in the ivermectin group; day 4 and day 8 in controls; larvae 24 to 362 per wound at detection.

Abstract

Introduction The re-emergence of the New World screwworm ( Cochliomyia hominivorax ) in the Americas represents a renewed challenge for livestock production, animal welfare, and regional surveillance systems. Myiasis caused by this obligate parasitic fly produces rapid tissue destruction, severe inflammation, and intense pain in affected animals, making its prevention a critical component of welfare-oriented livestock management. Despite the widespread use of macrocyclic lactones within livestock health programs, field-based epidemiological evidence describing the occurrence of screwworm infestation under natural exposure conditions remains limited. This study aimed to document the natural occurrence and characteristics of Cochliomyia hominivorax myiasis in surgically treated cattle exposed under endemic conditions while receiving different macrocyclic lactone regimens. Methods An observational field study was conducted in southern Mexico using Brahman × Simbrah crossbred cattle (12–16 months old). Animals were evaluated in two observation periods (November–December 2025 and January 2026) and allocated into three groups: untreated control, ivermectin (3.5%), and doramectin (1%). A standardized full-thickness surgical wound was created in each animal to allow natural oviposition by screwworm flies. Cattle were monitored for 21 days post-surgery for the occurrence of myiasis, larval burden severity, larval developmental stages, and wound progression. Recovered larvae were morphologically and morphometrically examined to confirm species identity and developmental stage. Results During the first observation period, myiasis occurred predominantly in ivermectin-treated cattle, with infestations detected as early as three days post-surgery and larval burdens frequently classified as severe. Two animals in the untreated control group developed myiasis on Day eight, whereas no infestations were observed in the doramectin-treated group. In the second observation period, infestation frequency decreased, with one case detected in both the control and ivermectin groups and none in the doramectin group. All recovered larvae corresponded to late second (L2) and third (L3) instars of Cochliomyia hominivorax and exhibited preserved morphology and high motility. Discussion These findings highlight the multifactorial nature of screwworm infestation under natural field conditions, including environmental variables and pharmacological context. The study provides epidemiologically relevant evidence that can contribute to risk assessment of myiasis occurrence, improvement of livestock surveillance systems, and evidence-based decision-making in integrated screwworm control policies aimed at protecting livestock health and welfare in regions facing the re-emergence of Cochliomyia hominivorax .

Quotes

Citation: Muchiut S, Miró MV, Anziani O, Nava S, Lifschitz A. Failure of doramectin and ivermectin in preventing Cochliomyia hominivorax myiasis in a subtropical region. Vet Parasitol 2025;334:110384.

Kind of evidence: experimental study also outbreak observation

An Argentine trial on castrated calves, wounds inspected on days 3, 6 and 13 only: 9 of 10 untreated wounds showed screwworm myiasis at the day-3 inspection.

Deliberate wounds in a treatment trial, but infestation came from wild flies (natural exposure).

Open the source

What it reports: Controls 9/10 by day 3.

Abstract

The aim of this work is to present a case study where the failure of IVM 3.15 % and DRM 1 % to prevent natural infestations of C. hominivorax larvae in Argentina is investigated based on field efficacy tests and a pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic analysis. Thirty male crossbred Braford calves were randomly assigned to three experimental groups (n = 10), the IVM 3.15 % group (subcutaneously at 630 µg/kg), the DRM 1 % group (subcutaneously at 200 µg/kg) and the control group (saline solution subcutaneously). All treatments were performed at the time of castration surgery through a scrotal incision, and the wounds were exposed to natural infestations of C. hominivorax. Wound inspections were carried out on days 3, 6, and 13 post-treatments. Jugular blood samples were taken from experimental animals at 3- and 6-days post-treatment. In presence of C. hominivorax larvae, samples of both the larvae and wound secretions were collected in plastic vials on days 3 and 6 to measure concentrations of both drugs by high-performance liquid chromatography. On day 3 post-treatment, active myiasis was observed in 9 animals from the control group, 5 from the IVM 3.15 % group, and 6 from the DRM 1 % group. On day 6 post-treatment, 5 and 3 new myiasis were detected in the IVM 3.15 % and DRM 1 % group, respectively. No larvae were observed in the wounds on day 13 post-treatment. Interestingly, DRM concentrations tended to be higher in larvae compared to IVM on day 3 post-treatment (p = 0.051), and IVM plasma concentrations tended to be higher than those measured for DRM on day 6 (p = 0.087). There was a very strong correlation between DRM and IVM concentrations in plasma and wound secretions and larvae. The uptake of DRM from wound secretions to larvae was 83 % greater than that of IVM (p = 0.03). The results of this trial suggest the presence of C. hominivorax resistance to DRM and highlight concern about the lack of effectiveness of IVM 3.15 % in preventing C. hominivorax infestations.

Abstract

An outbreak of New World screwworm has recently been spreading across Mexico, after more than 30 years of absence. The sterile insect technique, which consists of the massive release of sterilized males, has proven to be one of the most efficient methods for controlling the screwworm pest. However, given the limited number of sterile males available, improving the release strategy is critical. We propose a mathematical model of population dynamics adapted to the biology of Cochliomyia hominivorax and derive a feedback control function to determine the number of sterile males to release. We further construct a Luenberger observer to estimate wild fly populations from infected animal counts-the variable monitored by Mexican sanitary authorities-enabling field implementation of the control function. We show that eradication is achievable within approximately 60-100 weeks and that eradication time is governed primarily by the intrinsic biology of the system rather than by infestation magnitude. We then extend the model to a spatially explicit framework and show that when sterile male releases are applied at the outbreak focus and within a 120 km radius, eradication of the pest is attainable.

A-3.13 Moya-Borja GE, Oliveira CM, Muniz RA, Goncalves LC. Prophylactic and persistent efficacy of doramectin...

Citation: Moya-Borja GE, Oliveira CM, Muniz RA, Goncalves LC. Prophylactic and persistent efficacy of doramectin against Cochliomyia hominivorax in cattle. Vet Parasitol 1993;49(1):95-105.

Kind of evidence: experimental study

Primary or not: primary The source's own trial measurements.

A 1993 Brazilian trial (full text read): calves were given doramectin and, 2 hours later, two incisions each seeded with 50 first-stage larvae. Larvae were gone from treated wounds 24 to 48 hours after treatment and wounds healed by 96 to 120 hours. The dosing was preventive: the drug was in the animal before the larvae, so it does not time the clearing of an established wound.

Open the source

What it reports: First-instar larvae eliminated 24 to 48 h post-treatment; healing began at 24 h and was complete at 96 to 120 h; 100 percent of control incisions infested.

Abstract

Two prophylactic studies and one persistent efficacy study were conducted in Brazil to evaluate one injection of doramectin at a dose rate of 200 micrograms kg-1 against induced infestations of the New World screwworm, Cochliomyia hominivorax. In each prophylactic study, 12 calves were allocated to two groups of six animals. Six calves were treated with doramectin and six with saline. Two hours after treatment, animals were anesthetized and received two incisions, one in the shoulder and one in the rump. Each incision was then infested with 50 first instar larvae. In the persistent efficacy study, 24 calves were allocated to six groups (T1-T6) of four animals each. On the day of treatment, three groups (T1, T3 and T5) were treated with saline and three groups (T2, T4 and T6) with doramectin. All animals were anesthetized and received four incisions, one in the shoulder and one in the rump of each side. Each incision was then infested with 30 first instar larvae of C. hominivorax with the following schedule: T1 and T2 at Day 3, T3 and T4 at Day 7, and T5 and T6 at Day 14 post-treatment. Calves were observed daily and incisions evaluated for 8 days post-infection. Larvae that completed development and exited the wounds were collected and incubated to evaluate viability. In all experiments, doramectin was 100% efficacious in preventing screwworm infestation caused by field isolates of C. hominivorax. First instar larvae were eliminated from the incisions of doramectin-treated calves between 24 and 48 h post-treatment, and no third instar were recovered at any time. As a consequence, healing started at 24 h and was completed at 96-120 h post-infection. Screwworm infestations and viable third-instar larvae developed in all the incisions in non-treated calves, and healing did not begin until larvae had completed their normal life cycle and exited the wounds. The persistent efficacy of a single injection of doramectin extended beyond 14 days.

Abstract

Bovines are suitable hosts and can be affected by fly infestations. Flies pose a significant threat to cattle livestock in Latin America (LA), causing substantial economic repercussions to animal production (reduced productivity, veterinary expenses, and decreased animal welfare) and damage to human health. The most important flies affecting cattle in Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, Mexico, and Uruguay are Haematobia irritans, Dermatobia hominis, and Cochliomyia hominivorax. Due to production losses and the consequent economic costs associated with these flies, control measures must be implemented, primarily relying on insecticidal products. However, decision-making for preventing and treating animals with insecticides varies due to differences in environmental conditions across countries and regions, production systems, animal populations, infestation levels, animal welfare, and the prevalence of myiasis, among other factors. Although insecticides remain the most effective option for fly control in cattle, resistant populations have developed, rendering them less effective. To overcome fly resistance to insecticides, non-chemical (mechanical, environmental, biological, and genetic) methods are being integrated into alternative control and eradication strategies. The use of integrated livestock fly control contributes to safeguarding animal, public, and environmental health. This review is designed to support individuals and institutions, both civil and governmental, addressing the ongoing challenge posed by flies affecting livestock.

Abstract

Before its eradication from North America, the subtropical-tropical new world screwworm fly Cochliomyia hominivorax (Coquerel) invaded southwestern temperate areas of the U.S.A., where it caused myiasis in wildlife and livestock. Outbreaks of the fly occurred during years when adult migrants were carried northward on North American monsoon winds from the northern areas of Mexico and south Texas. We deconstruct, retrospectively, the biology and the effect of weather on the eradication of the fly in North America. Screwworm was found to be an ideal candidate for eradication using the sterile insect technique (SIT) because females mate only once, whereas males are polygynous, and, although it has a high reproductive potential, field population growth rates are low in tropical areas. In northern areas, eradication was enhanced by cool-cold weather, whereas eradication in tropical Mexico and Central America is explained by the SIT. Despite low average efficacy of SIT releases (approximately 1.7%), the added pressure of massive SIT releases reduced intrinsically low fly populations, leading to mate-limited extinction. Non-autochthonous cases of myiasis occur in North America and, if the fly reestablishes, climate warming by 2045-2055 will expand the area of favourability and increase the frequency and severity of outbreaks.

Abstract

Objectives To compare the sensitivity of inspections of cattle herds and adult fly trapping for detection of the Old World screw-worm fly (OWS). Procedures The incidence of myiases on animals and the number of OWS trapped with LuciTrap®/Bezzilure were measured concurrently on cattle farms on Sumba Island (Indonesia) and in peninsular Malaysia (two separate periods for the latter). The numbers of animal inspections and traps required to achieve OWS detection at the prevalent fly densities were calculated. Results On Sumba Island, with low-density OWS populations, the sensitivity of herd inspections and of trapping for OWS detection was 0.30 and 0.85, respectively. For 95% confidence of detecting OWS, either 45 inspections of 74 animals or trapping with 5 sets of 4 LuciTraps for 14 days are required. In Malaysia, at higher OWS density, herd inspections of 600 animals (twice weekly, period 1) or 1600 animals (weekly, period 2) always detected myiases (sensitivity = 1), while trapping had sensitivities of 0.89 and 0.64 during periods 1 and 2, respectively. For OWS detection with 95% confidence, fewer than 600 and 1600 animals or 2 and 6 LuciTraps are required in periods 1 and 2, respectively. Conclusions Inspections of cattle herds and trapping with LuciTrap and Bezzilure can detect OWS populations. As a preliminary guide for OWS detection in Australia, the numbers of animals and traps derived from the Sumba Island trial should be used because the prevailing conditions better match those of northern Australia.

C-1.1 Gutierrez AP, Ponti L, Arias PA. Deconstructing the eradication of New World screwworm in North America:...

Citation: Gutierrez AP, Ponti L, Arias PA. Deconstructing the eradication of New World screwworm in North America: retrospective analysis and climate warming effects. Med Vet Entomol 2019;33(2):282-295.

Kind of evidence: model or expert estimate

Primary or not: secondary Model paper; the figures used here are cited from other studies.

The 2019 population model citing tropical field doubling of 54 to 139 days, female dispersal of about 3 km, and historic sterile release rates.

The 54 to 139 d range is cited from Matlock and Skoda 2009 (C-1.2).

Open the source

What it reports: endemic tropical field doubling 54 to 139 d (Matlock and Skoda 2009); potential doubling 14 d; female dispersal about 3 km, 10 to 20 km reported, 300 km in arid wind-aided settings; historic weekly releases 39 to 896 sterile flies per km2 (Matlock et al. 1996); 1,890 sterile flies released per case of myiasis; about 67 eggs per female per day maximum; thermal window 14.5 to 43.5 C, optimum about 27.5 C; simulated bi-weekly releases of 2 sterile flies per km2 sufficed for eradication at McAllen because the modelled wild population was intrinsically low

Abstract

Before its eradication from North America, the subtropical-tropical new world screwworm fly Cochliomyia hominivorax (Coquerel) invaded southwestern temperate areas of the U.S.A., where it caused myiasis in wildlife and livestock. Outbreaks of the fly occurred during years when adult migrants were carried northward on North American monsoon winds from the northern areas of Mexico and south Texas. We deconstruct, retrospectively, the biology and the effect of weather on the eradication of the fly in North America. Screwworm was found to be an ideal candidate for eradication using the sterile insect technique (SIT) because females mate only once, whereas males are polygynous, and, although it has a high reproductive potential, field population growth rates are low in tropical areas. In northern areas, eradication was enhanced by cool-cold weather, whereas eradication in tropical Mexico and Central America is explained by the SIT. Despite low average efficacy of SIT releases (approximately 1.7%), the added pressure of massive SIT releases reduced intrinsically low fly populations, leading to mate-limited extinction. Non-autochthonous cases of myiasis occur in North America and, if the fly reestablishes, climate warming by 2045-2055 will expand the area of favourability and increase the frequency and severity of outbreaks.

Quotes

However, in the tropics, growth rates of endemic field population are low (Thomas & Mangan, 1992) with field doubling times ranging from 54 to 139 days (Matlock & Skoda, 2009)

C-1.2 Matlock RB, Skoda SR. Mark-recapture estimates of recruitment, survivorship and population growth rate for...

Citation: Matlock RB, Skoda SR. Mark-recapture estimates of recruitment, survivorship and population growth rate for the screwworm fly, Cochliomyia hominivorax. Med Vet Entomol 2009;23(2):111-125.

Kind of evidence: experimental study

Primary or not: primary The source's own mark-recapture field study.

A 2009 mark-recapture study of screwworm flies in Costa Rica (19,573 released) estimating daily growth of 1.005, a doubling time of about 139 days.

Field mark-recapture of released flies; estimates wild population growth.

What it reports: eight mark-recapture studies, Costa Rica, 19,573 released, 4,476 recaptured; phi = 0.798 (0.008), f = 0.193 (0.008), lambda = 1.005 (0.002) per day; doubling time from lambda 139 d

Abstract

Pradel model mark-release-recapture estimates of survivorship, phi, recruitment, f, and the rate of density-independent population growth, lambda, are presented for eight mark-recapture studies of the screwworm Cochliomyia hominivorax (Coquerel) (Diptera: Calliphoridae) from Costa Rica, totalling 19 573 released and 4476 recaptured flies. Corroborative estimates of survivorship and the rate of population growth based on an extensive review of the literature are also reported. Weighted-mean +/- standard error of the mean (SEM) mark-release-recapture estimates of survivorship, recruitment and the rate of population growth were phi = 0.798 +/- 0.008, f = 0.193 +/- 0.008 and lambda = 1.005 +/- 0.002, respectively. Population doubling time was estimated from lambda at 139 days. Estimates of phi and lambda from the literature both exceeded those calculated by mark-recapture methods and estimates of population doubling times were consequently shorter.

Quotes

the weighted-mean mark-release-recapture estimates of survivorship, recruitment and the rate of population growth were phi = 0.798 +/- 0.008, f = 0.193 +/- 0.008 and lambda = 1.005 +/- 0.002

C-2.6 Reyes R, Barrio RA. A mathematical model for the efficient control of the New World screwworm. PLoS One...

Citation: Reyes R, Barrio RA. A mathematical model for the efficient control of the New World screwworm. PLoS One 2026;21(8):e0355963.

Kind of evidence: model or expert estimate

Primary or not: unclear A modelling assumption, not an observation or a summary of others.

The 2026 Mexico outbreak model: one random long-distance introduction about every 61 days, seeded anywhere on its whole grid (the state of Chiapas). Its fit to the case map is weak (mean Jaccard index 0.17).

Open the source

What it reports: lambda_seed = 0.1143 events per week, one long-distance introduction per 8.75 weeks (61 d), each at a random cell of the whole modelled grid (50 by 50 cells of about 8 km over the state of Chiapas, roughly 400 km across). The 120 km radius in the paper is its sterile-fly release zone, not the seeding domain.

Abstract

An outbreak of New World screwworm has recently been spreading across Mexico, after more than 30 years of absence. The sterile insect technique, which consists of the massive release of sterilized males, has proven to be one of the most efficient methods for controlling the screwworm pest. However, given the limited number of sterile males available, improving the release strategy is critical. We propose a mathematical model of population dynamics adapted to the biology of Cochliomyia hominivorax and derive a feedback control function to determine the number of sterile males to release. We further construct a Luenberger observer to estimate wild fly populations from infected animal counts-the variable monitored by Mexican sanitary authorities-enabling field implementation of the control function. We show that eradication is achievable within approximately 60-100 weeks and that eradication time is governed primarily by the intrinsic biology of the system rather than by infestation magnitude. We then extend the model to a spatially explicit framework and show that when sterile male releases are applied at the outbreak focus and within a 120 km radius, eradication of the pest is attainable.

C-4.4 Skoda SR, Phillips PL, Welch JB. Screwworm (Diptera: Calliphoridae) in the United States: response to and...

Citation: Skoda SR, Phillips PL, Welch JB. Screwworm (Diptera: Calliphoridae) in the United States: response to and elimination of the 2016-2017 outbreak in Florida. J Med Entomol 2018;55(4):777-786.

Kind of evidence: outbreak observation also model or expert estimate

Primary or not: primary The responders' own outbreak account; the wild fly density is an estimate.

The 2018 Florida outbreak account: estimated wild density over 1,250 flies per square km, about 2.65 million sterile flies a week, and the last fertile fly 27 days after releases began.

The wild density is an estimate.

Open the source

What it reports: standard ratio 10 sterile to 1 fertile; estimated wild density more than 1,250 flies per km2 on Big Pine Key, so about 12,500 per km2 needed; about 2,653,920 sterile flies released weekly at the epicenter (the extraction gives the release area as about 25.8 km2, so about 100,000 per km2 per week, roughly 80:1); eradication effort began 11 October 2016, last fertile fly 7 November (27 days); 13 keys positive by 28 October out of 43 sampled, all west of the Seven Mile Bridge; releases continued to 25 April 2017 because of Key deer fawning

Abstract

Eradicating screwworm, Cochliomyia hominivorax (Coquerel), from continental North American via the sterile insect technique has provided huge economic benefit to livestock producers by eliminating screwworm myiasis. After confirmatory identification of fly samples from infested deer by the USDA National Veterinary Services Laboratory on September 30, 2016, an alert was issued that screwworm myiasis was discovered in the Florida Keys. Personnel from USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, Agricultural Research Service, the State of Florida, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and local officials responded to the outbreak focus on Big Pine Key. After witnessing infested Key deer (Odocoileus virginianus clavium Barboyr & Allen), screwworm adult sampling was initiated at 0930 h on October 5, 2016 using nets to collect flies arriving at putrid liver, with the first female collected within 1 h. Larval samples were collected from infested animals for DNA analyses and to develop a "Florida outbreak" colony to test mating compatibility with the mass-produced strain used for sterile fly releases. Ground release chambers for sterile screwworm releases were placed in favorable habitats based on satellite image analyses. Sterile pupae were first placed in the chambers on October 11, 2016. Further liver trapping showed that 13 Keys were infested. One case, presumably through animal movement, occurred near Homestead on the Florida mainland. Ultimately there were 35 sterile fly release stations, including 4 located around Homestead, but no further cases were identified. About 188 million sterile flies were released until successful eradication was declared on March 23, 2017. Containing the outbreak prevented economic losses to livestock producers and other wildlife on the mainland and kept eradication costs to a minimum.
